full_judgment: 40. One of the cardinal principles which has always to be kept in mind in our system of administration of justice in criminal cases is that, an accused is presumed to be innocent unless that presumption is rebutted by the prosecution by production of evidences as may show him to be guilty of the offence with which he charged. The burden of proving the guilty of the accused is always upon the prosecution and unless it relives itself of that burden, the court cannot be a record finding of guilt of the accused. Criminality is never presumed. Against order of acquittal it is to be kept in mind that there is a presumption of innocence in favour of the accused person and the trial Court having acquitted him the said presumption is to be considered to have been further strengthened. In applying the presumption of innocence the High Court Division is definitely slow to disturb the findings based upon appreciation of oral evidence. The correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the trial Court or the Tribunal, it is true, is the subject matter of the appeal and is therefore open to the examination by the High Court Division but while assessing the evidences, the High Court Division must not ignore the opinion of the trial Court or the Tribunal before reversing an order under appeal, more so in an order against acquittal. Unless the conclusions reached by the court or the Tribunal are palpably based upon an erroneous view of the law or the decision is likely to result in grave injustice, the High Court Division would be reluctant to interfere with the said decision. Again an order of acquittal can only be blown away if the same can be characterised as perverse or the court or Tribunal has misdirected itself so as to carry a miscarriage of justice. This is the broad approach before the High Court Division in hearing appeals against order of acquittal.
